First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
arxiv:2611.03066.tldr: Examines the Internet of Agentics architectural perspective, organizing protocols like MCP and A2A for interoperable multi-agent systems.
arxiv:2611.03066.why: Good architectural overview of emerging agent standards like MCP that you might adopt in enterprise systems.

arxiv:2611.02286.title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
arxiv:2611.02286.abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.
arxiv:2611.02286.tldr: Reviews data structures and interoperability challenges for agentic AI workflows in the built environment, highlighting RAG and MCP.
arxiv:2611.02286.why: Provides practical context on combining structured and unstructured sources for enterprise RAG and agent workflows.

arxiv:2611.03344.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell
arxiv:2611.03344.abstract: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of 1.10--1.40times on B200 and 1.06--1.42times on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.
arxiv:2611.03344.summary_hint: FLAMIA accelerates Transformer attention on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs via MXFP8 and mixed-precision kernels that reduce quantization overhead, prevent causal leakage, and support variable-length packed documents.
arxiv:2611.03344.tldr: Presents FLAMIA, attention kernels for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs supporting MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths.
arxiv:2611.03344.why: Too hardware-specific and focused on pre-training/training attention kernels rather than application-layer inference.

arxiv:2611.03138.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL
arxiv:2611.03138.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
arxiv:2611.03138.tldr: Introduces KlaskTron, a low-cost physical tabletop robotic testbed and digital twin for adversarial multi-agent RL.
arxiv:2611.03138.why: Completely off-topic robotics hardware and reinforcement learning research.

arxiv:2611.01386.title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
arxiv:2611.01386.abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.
arxiv:2611.01386.tldr: Presents Zep Agent Skills, a production procedural memory service that compiles verified execution traces into versioned skills.
arxiv:2611.01386.why: Directly applicable pattern for adding persistent procedural memory and skill refinement to production agent systems.

arxiv:2611.03197.title: Finding the Pivots to Repair Broken Source-Test Evolution Using LLMs
arxiv:2611.03197.abstract: Repairing obsolete tests in response to source code evolution is critical for test suite reliability and software quality assurance. While large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools for automating many software development tasks, the effective supply of context and the orchestration of repair pipelines in this source--test co-evolution scenario remain poorly understood. Moreover, although reasoning is found helpful for LLMs on some complex coding tasks, it remains unclear which reasoning steps actually contribute to effective test repairs and how the insights learned from LLMs' behaviors benefit coding agents. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical study of test repair for source-test co-evolution empowered by LLMs, investigating the effective setups and typical LLM behaviors. To support this study, we construct a new benchmark of 500 real-world source-test co-evolution cases from commits submitted between May 2024 and April 2026 across 15 highly-starred open-source Java projects. Our experimental results reveal several key insights for effective LLM-based test repair: the complementary benefits of combining test failure symptoms, source code changes, and supportive code context, as well as the effectiveness of self-repair rounds. We further derive a common reasoning action taxonomy from LLMs' reasoning traces, which proves instrumental in guiding LLMs to repair tests more effectively while at a lower financial cost. Applying our findings to the Codex agent further improves its repair success rate on challenging cases by 66.7%.
arxiv:2611.03197.tldr: Empirically studies test repair for source-test co-evolution using LLMs across a new benchmark of 500 Java cases.
arxiv:2611.03197.why: Provides empirical insights into effective context and orchestration setups for automated software engineering agents.

arxiv:2611.02383.title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
arxiv:2611.02383.abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction
arxiv:2611.02383.tldr: Analyzes 3,387 instruction files across four formats (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, etc.) and derives an evidence-based template.
arxiv:2611.02383.why: Useful guidelines for structuring repository-level context and instruction files when building coding or developer agents.

arxiv:2611.03526.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
arxiv:2611.03526.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
arxiv:2611.03526.summary_hint: Library of Layers dynamically orders transformer blocks during inference to adapt computation to tasks, enabling parameter reuse, sparsity, and interpretable routing across reasoning, multilingual, and safety settings.
arxiv:2611.03526.tldr: Introduces Library of Layers, a transformer architecture that dynamically orders layers at runtime, trading off efficiency and sparsity.
arxiv:2611.03526.why: Novel runtime architecture, but changes core model weights and inference engines, making it impractical for standard production cloud LLM stacks.

arxiv:2611.02633.title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
arxiv:2611.02633.abstract: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.
arxiv:2611.02633.summary_hint: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark evaluates AI agents as teammates across 240 tasks, revealing that even top models have significant collaboration weaknesses unrelated to individual capability.
arxiv:2611.02633.tldr: Introduces a Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark with 240 tasks across 8 teamwork dimensions to measure how well AI agents act as teammates.
arxiv:2611.02633.why: Useful evaluation framing and test cases for multi-agent orchestration systems, though mostly an evaluation benchmark rather than a deployable tool.

arxiv:2611.01815.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
arxiv:2611.01815.abstract: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
arxiv:2611.01815.summary_hint: The study evaluates frozen video representations to show that prediction errors reflect appearance and motion rather than reliably measuring physical surprise.
arxiv:2611.01815.tldr: Evaluates when latent prediction errors in video world models genuinely reflect physical surprise versus static visual changes.
arxiv:2611.01815.why: Purely focused on video world models and physical surprise benchmarks, completely unrelated to enterprise LLM apps or RAG.

arxiv:2611.02112.title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
arxiv:2611.02112.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.
arxiv:2611.02112.summary_hint: Order-only on-policy distillation trains students to match teacher token rankings rather than probabilities, improving reasoning performance without temperature tuning.
arxiv:2611.02112.tldr: Proposes Order-Only On-Policy Distillation, which trains student models using only the token ranking order of teacher models, removing temperature sensitivity.
arxiv:2611.02112.why: Interesting post-training distillation technique for smaller models, but post-training is outside your typical day-to-day app engineering scope.

arxiv:2611.02332.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
arxiv:2611.02332.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.
arxiv:2611.02332.summary_hint: LeanGuard is a verified runtime that blocks policy-violating tool calls by language-model agents and can repair them via proof-guided search, reducing unauthorized executions and prompt-injection success without harming benign task performance.
arxiv:2611.02332.tldr: Presents LeanGuard, a runtime that validates agent tool calls against Lean4 formal policies, eliminating forbidden actions and reducing prompt injection.
arxiv:2611.02332.why: Highly relevant security and reliability pattern for production tool-using agents; provides robust fail-closed guardrails against unsafe tool calls.

arxiv:2611.02797.title: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents
arxiv:2611.02797.abstract: Recursively self-improving (RSI) systems are increasingly viewed as a promising means of accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. They aim to autonomously improve their capabilities by refining their working pipelines and recursively improving the strategies that guide subsequent refinements, with gains generalizing to unseen scenarios.However, existing evaluations lack reliable metrics to distinguish capability gains from scenario fitting, sustainable and extensible protocols for unseen tasks and difficulties, and fine-grained attribution of improvement to evolution traces. To this end, we propose SelfImprove-Bench,an RSI evaluation framework that organizes tasks into three primary capabilities (i.e., Exploring, Planning, Reasoning) as scenarios for guiding model evolution. We instantiated the tasks on games for controllability and reproducibility, and pairs them with scalable generation and orchestration driven by task templates and difficulty coefficients. Beyond task-level scores, SelfImprove-Bench organizes evaluation into generalization ladder levels G0 to G4 that measure how far gains transfer from training conditions. Experiments reveal that the evolutionary gains of existing RSI methods are inconsistent across generalization levels.
arxiv:2611.02797.tldr: Proposes SelfImprove-Bench to evaluate recursively self-improving agents across exploring, planning, and reasoning tasks.
arxiv:2611.02797.why: Provides evaluation concepts for advanced agent loops, but focuses heavily on recursive self-improvement rather than practical enterprise orchestration.

arxiv:2611.01351.title: MAPLE: A Multimodal Mobile Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience
arxiv:2611.01351.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) show great potential in navigating mobile graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete complex tasks. However, existing paradigms face fundamental scalability bottlenecks: fine-tuning requires massive high-fidelity datasets or prohibitive training time and compute, while gradient-free approaches rely on custom static heuristics or costly trial-and-error trajectory exploration where feedback is deferred until the end of execution. To address these limitations, we introduce MAPLE (Multimodal Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience), a novel gradient-free multi-agent framework that enables dynamic, step-wise experience sharing and execution-time prompt evolution. Unlike traditional action-reflection architectures that depend on costly, post-hoc self-reflection, MAPLE enables agents to cross-reference and distribute runtime insights in real time at each operational step. This dynamic exchange eliminates blind trial-and-error looping and steers agents along direct, grounded interaction paths. Extensive evaluations on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex, long-horizon mobile tasks, while proving scalable and adaptable across novel environments.
arxiv:2611.01351.tldr: Introduces MAPLE, a gradient-free multi-agent framework for mobile GUIs that shares execution insights in real time via playbooks.
arxiv:2611.01351.why: Demonstrates real-time experience sharing and prompt evolution patterns across agents, applicable to complex multi-agent enterprise workflows.

arxiv:2611.00638.title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
arxiv:2611.00638.abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.
arxiv:2611.00638.tldr: Combines hybrid document parsing with vision LLMs to extract structured records from scientific PDFs, achieving 0.97 F1 score.
arxiv:2611.00638.why: Relevant architectural pattern and evaluation benchmark for heavy document processing and extraction pipelines dealing with complex layouts.

arxiv:2611.03634.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
arxiv:2611.03634.abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.
arxiv:2611.03634.tldr: Provides WebHarbor, a suite of 153 dockerized website environments with 3,518 tasks for evaluating and training web GUI agents.
arxiv:2611.03634.why: Useful testing ground if you build web-scraping or browser automation agents, but likely too niche for general RAG and enterprise search.

arxiv:2611.02810.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
arxiv:2611.02810.abstract: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.
arxiv:2611.02810.tldr: Proposes TRIO, an iterative RAG framework using three cooperative agents for query expansion, retrieval sufficiency voting, and answer refinement.
arxiv:2611.02810.why: Directly applicable multi-agent RAG pattern to improve retrieval quality and reduce hallucinations via iterative query and answer refinement.

arxiv:2611.02387.title: EviCast: Forecasting Retrieval Gains Through Shared Response Calibration
arxiv:2611.02387.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) extends large language models with external evidence, yet relevant evidence does not ensure that a generator can use it. Indiscriminate retrieval can degrade task performance while adding retrieval and long-context inference costs. Existing methods neither determine before large-scale execution whether a generator, task distribution, and retriever configuration is worth deploying nor diagnose multiple candidate retrievers under a shared budget. We introduce EviCast, a framework that forecasts retrieval value through interventional evidence-state decomposition. EviCast measures a generator's response to controlled evidence states once and combines this shared profile with the offline evidence-state distribution of each candidate retriever, yielding the end-to-end net utility and its 95% lower confidence bound without executing every RAG configuration. A state-refinement analysis characterizes when its binary and topology-aware instantiations are exact and when shared calibration is statistically more efficient than per-retriever calibration. In frozen evaluations, EviCast correctly decides all 14 HotpotQA retrieval configurations with a forecast error of 2.75 F1 points while reducing diagnostic generation calls by 80%, and it attains the lowest forecast error among seven predictors in the low-budget regime. Its topology-aware instantiation, EviCast-T, captures the complementarity between terminal and bridge evidence, correctly deciding all 16 configurations on MuSiQue and HotpotQA and 23 of 24 after prospective transfer to a third dataset. These results show that retrieval deployment depends on both evidence availability and the generator's ability to convert evidence structure into stable net utility. Code is available at https://github.com/YiboWang2002/EviCast.
arxiv:2611.02387.tldr: Introduced EviCast, a framework that forecasts RAG retrieval value and net utility using interventional evidence-state decomposition without executing every candidate configuration.
arxiv:2611.02387.why: Directly useful for evaluating and selecting retriever configurations and cutting RAG pipeline costs before deployment.

arxiv:2611.02368.title: Beyond Accuracy: How Quantization Affects Coding Agents
arxiv:2611.02368.abstract: Agents are increasingly used for coding tasks, but the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) limits where they can run. Quantization reduces model size, but its effects on coding agents that execute and revise programs remain underexplored. We compare BF16 with 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B, 14B, and 32B) and Devstral-Small-2507 (24B) on OJBench coding problems across three seeds. We detect no statistically significant accuracy loss for any of the coding agents. However, final accuracy can conceal substantial behavioral changes: AWQ reduces Qwen-7B one-shot solves from 17 to 0 while increasing loop-based solves from 10 to 25. All Qwen-32B successes involve tool use, whereas Devstral rarely makes a valid executor call. Failure profiles also differ: Qwen-32B produces far more compilation errors than the smaller Qwen models, rising slightly under quantization, while Devstral's failures shift significantly from runtime errors toward wrong answers and timeouts. These findings indicate that quantization robustness in coding agents should be assessed through solution trajectories, tool use, and failure modes, in addition to final accuracy.
arxiv:2611.02368.tldr: Evaluated how 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ quantization affect coding agents on OJBench, finding no accuracy loss but substantial shifts in tool use and failure profiles.
arxiv:2611.02368.why: Provides cautionary evaluation insights for quantizing LLMs used in agentic coding and multi-step tool-use workflows.

arxiv:2611.02121.title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
arxiv:2611.02121.abstract: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.
arxiv:2611.02121.tldr: Studied conditional calibration contracts and load-coupled routing for switched inference serving architectures under bursty loads.
arxiv:2611.02121.why: Relevant background on router reliability and calibration under production load, though heavily theoretical.

arxiv:2611.02104.title: Consolidating Reasoning with Test-Time Training
arxiv:2611.02104.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires finalizing solutions from reasoning that is distributed across the individual attempts of many agents. However, useful intermediate reasoning can remain unexploited when collaboration is limited to voting on conclusions reached among individual agents, or aggregating long, noisy collections of reasoning trajectories in context. In this work, we propose TTT-Consolidate, a framework that uses multi-agent reasoning trajectories as adaptation data to improve a model's subsequent reasoning. TTT-Consolidate jointly consolidates trajectories into parametric representations through test-time training, then generates a new solution by conditioning on the consolidated information. We meta-learn how to consolidate using bi-level optimization at training time, where an inner loop encodes reasoning trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and an outer loop learns meta-parameters for the inner loop such that the consolidation is helpful for the model to synthesize a final solution. As no large-scale corpus of diverse reasoning trajectories exists for training aggregation methods, we construct the OpenParallelThinking corpus composed of 12,810 math problems paired with a mixture of trajectories from six LLMs. Evaluated on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points, even under matched compute and runtime settings, with the gap widening at larger model scales. TTT-Consolidate also recovers from unsuccessful individual trajectories more robustly, an ability that improves as the number of available (even incorrect) trajectories increases. Finally, we demonstrate that TTT-Consolidate benefits from both SFT and RL-based outer loop objectives. We will release TTT-Consolidate and OpenParallelThinking for use in future work on reasoning aggregation.
arxiv:2611.02104.tldr: Proposed TTT-Consolidate, using test-time training to adaptively consolidate multi-agent reasoning trajectories into lightweight LoRA adapters for final synthesis.
arxiv:2611.02104.why: Offers an advanced post-training technique for improving multi-agent reasoning aggregation beyond simple voting.

arxiv:2611.02011.title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
arxiv:2611.02011.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.
arxiv:2611.02011.tldr: Introduced MedPsy, 1.7B and 4B medical language models optimized via synthetic data and reinforcement learning for edge deployment.
arxiv:2611.02011.why: Too domain-specific (medical) for general enterprise RAG and agent architectures.

arxiv:2611.01778.title: MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents
arxiv:2611.01778.abstract: LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character's style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but do not reason about how past events shape a character's current motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.
arxiv:2611.01778.tldr: Proposed MemRole, a framework for long-horizon narrative role-playing agents that structures memory-to-decision processes and self-refining distillation.
arxiv:2611.01778.why: Narrowly focused on character role-playing narratives rather than enterprise agent applications.

arxiv:2611.01415.title: Latent Harness: Compiling Agent Behaviors into Post-Block Activation Shifts
arxiv:2611.01415.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
arxiv:2611.01415.tldr: Presented Latent Harness, which compiles external agentic prompt harnesses into rank-8 activation shifts applied across decoder blocks, eliminating runtime prompt overhead.
arxiv:2611.01415.why: Potentially cuts per-call token costs and latency for complex agent prompt harnesses in production.

arxiv:2611.00871.title: ShiftRAG: Bypassing the Textual Bottleneck via Decoupled Learning and Continuous Soft Tokens
arxiv:2611.00871.abstract: Despite advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), suppressing hallucinations during complex reasoning remains a persistent challenge. We identify that existing RAG pipelines suffer from a textual bottleneck: by passing only raw text to the generator, they discard discriminative signals of the retriever. Furthermore, recent attempts to unify retrieval and generation within a single LLM induce severe objective conflict and exacerbate the rank collapse of decoder-only architectures, degrading performance on both tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce ShiftRAG, a decoupled RAG framework that employs a single LLM backbone but isolates discriminative retrieval learning from autoregressive generation. To bridge these decoupled modes, we project retrieval alignments into continuous soft tokens, establishing a high-bandwidth interface that infuses the generator with retrieval-side signals. Concurrently, our soft orthogonality objective mitigates rank collapse, while layer-wise relevance dynamics preserve the fine-grained latent space required for highly discriminative evidence separation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that ShiftRAG significantly improves retrieval and question answering performance over state-of-the-art baselines. ShiftRAG preserves foundational capabilities of the backbone while maintaining a favorable efficiency-performance trade-off on general text encoding and generative tasks.
arxiv:2611.00871.tldr: Introduced ShiftRAG, a decoupled RAG framework using continuous soft tokens to pass retrieval-side signals into the generator without textual bottlenecks.
arxiv:2611.00871.why: Provides a novel architectural pattern to improve RAG grounding and bypass the textual generation bottleneck.

arxiv:2611.03534.title: An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment
arxiv:2611.03534.abstract: Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent's tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33-67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.
arxiv:2611.03534.tldr: Presented Grid Agents, an ontology-backed agent system for automated power system studies and grid connection assessment.
arxiv:2611.03534.why: Too domain-specific (power systems engineering) to transfer directly to general enterprise LLM apps.

arxiv:2611.03116.title: From Local Skills to Long-Horizon Web Tasks: Progressive Skill Exploration for LLM Web Agents
arxiv:2611.03116.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are driving autonomous agents toward real-world environments, with the Web emerging as one of the most representative interaction scenarios. However, training Web agents with naive exploration remains challenging: successful trajectories are rare, and the sparse terminal rewards make it difficult for agents to obtain useful feedback from failed trajectories. Inspired by skill acquisition theory, we propose Skill-Composed Progressive Exploration (SCOPE), a short-to-long learning framework for long-horizon Web agents that decomposes complex task exploration into a gradual expansion process from local skills to complete task-solving capability. Specifically, SCOPE iteratively explores around local skills: Skill Discovery extracts reusable local skills and failure experiences from historical rollouts; Skill Orchestration composes discovered skills into high-level skill chains; and Skill Expansion leverages failure experiences aligned with the current skill chain to guide the agent toward exploring new subskills. Through this process, SCOPE progressively constructs task-completing skill chains across rollouts and internalizes them into the policy parameters through agentic on-policy distillation. Extensive experiments on WebArena, WebVoyager, and WebShop show that SCOPE consistently improves exploration dynamics and achieves 3.9% to 18.6% relative gains over the strongest baselines in each setting.
arxiv:2611.03116.tldr: Proposed SCOPE, a progressive exploration framework that discovers local web-agent skills and composes them into high-level skill chains to solve long-horizon tasks.
arxiv:2611.03116.why: Useful background on skill discovery and composition for building reliable multi-step agents.

arxiv:2611.03005.title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
arxiv:2611.03005.abstract: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
arxiv:2611.03005.tldr: Introduces BLPO, a stepwise reinforcement learning method for long-horizon LLM agents that uses global memory and shared task-progress advantages without a learned critic.
arxiv:2611.03005.why: Relevant background for multi-agent orchestration and policy optimization, though tailored to training rather than applied application architecture.

arxiv:2611.02833.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
arxiv:2611.02833.abstract: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.
arxiv:2611.02833.tldr: Evaluates LLM agent performance on reproducing computational quantum science papers, finding they often fail without expert human intervention.
arxiv:2611.02833.why: Domain-specific evaluation of scientific reproducibility agents, lacking direct transfer to enterprise software or RAG workloads.

arxiv:2611.02784.title: HLSClaw: Bringing Vibe Coding to High-Level Synthesis through Skill-Based Agentic Harness
arxiv:2611.02784.abstract: LLM agents are rapidly shifting software development toward intent-driven \emph{vibe coding}, yet their effectiveness drops sharply in high-level synthesis (HLS), where code optimization must jointly consider design structure, directive search, and downstream hardware constraints. Existing HLS optimization approaches, including both heuristic-based methods and recent LLM-assisted pipelines, typically operate at fixed abstraction levels or in weakly coupled stages, limiting their ability to leverage the strong interplay between source code restructuring and directive search outcomes. Our key insight is that HLS optimization can be reframed from a fixed, hardwired transformation pipeline into a skill-based agentic control problem: an LLM agent equipped with modular, executable optimization skills and a feedback-driven orchestrator can autonomously navigate the coupled space of code restructuring and directive search. This motivates the design of HLSClaw, the first HLS-specific, skill-based agentic harness for holistic HLS optimization. On real-world HLS benchmarks, HLSClaw achieves a 39.12x geometric-mean latency speedup, outperforming the compiler baseline ScaleHLS by 1.98x, and surpassing the commercial coding agents Claude Code and Codex by 1.86x and 1.70x, respectively, while maintaining strong timing robustness.
arxiv:2611.02784.tldr: Presents HLSClaw, a skill-based agentic harness for holistic high-level synthesis optimization in hardware design.
arxiv:2611.02784.why: Too narrow and hardware-specific for general enterprise LLM engineering.

arxiv:2611.02725.title: AffToM: Benchmarking Recursive Affective Theory of Mind in Dynamic Multi-Party Interactions
arxiv:2611.02725.abstract: Understanding emotion in realistic social interactions requires more than recognizing facial expressions or assigning affective labels. The same event can elicit different emotions depending on what each participant knows, what they believe others know or feel, and how these nested mental states evolve over time. Existing benchmarks largely study higher-order epistemic Theory of Mind (ToM) and multimodal emotion reasoning in isolation, leaving recursive affective reasoning under asymmetric and dynamically changing information underexplored. Therefore, we introduce AffToM, a benchmark for affective ToM with 1,922 test pairs and 19,759 training pairs. AffToM evaluates Individual Affective Reasoning (IAR), which infers emotions from events and socio-cognitive context, and Multi-party Affective Reasoning (MPAR), which recursively tracks participants' nested beliefs and emotions as new evidence emerges. We develop an event-driven multi-agent generation pipeline grounded in dynamic character interaction graphs that explicitly capture event sequences, interpersonal relations, and mental-state updates. Furthermore, we propose AffToM-R1, a two-stage post-training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with perspective-aware rubric-guided reinforcement learning. Experiments show that MPAR remains challenging, with even the strongest evaluated MLLM achieving less than 60% accuracy, while AffToM-R1 improves MPAR accuracy by 13.38 percentage points over its base model. Our dataset is available at: https://github.com/MindIntLab-HFUT/AffToM.
arxiv:2611.02725.tldr: Introduces AffToM, a benchmark for evaluating recursive affective theory of mind in dynamic multi-party interactions.
arxiv:2611.02725.why: Focuses on social and emotional reasoning benchmarks, which are outside standard enterprise search and RAG applications.

arxiv:2611.02601.title: Parallelism-Aligned Pruning and Round-Aware Context Reuse for On-Device Multimodal Agents
arxiv:2611.02601.abstract: On-device multimodal agents are limited by two deployment mismatches: pretrained attention structures may not divide evenly across the compute cores of an edge accelerator, causing irregular partitions; and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, whose capacity grows with the number of rounds. We present PARC, which combines parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization. At the model level, it uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection to make attention dimensions divisible by the target core count while preserving the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension. At runtime, it separates the system prompt, persistent text history, and transient visual observations by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so that historical images leave the persistent cache and more interaction rounds fit a fixed budget. On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, hardware-aligned pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%; a parameter-matched control confirms that the speedup stems mainly from core alignment rather than parameter reduction.
arxiv:2611.02601.tldr: Proposes PARC, combining parallelism-aligned structured pruning and lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization for on-device multimodal agents, cutting unnecessary image persistence.
arxiv:2611.02601.why: Useful techniques for KV-cache management and optimizing inference latency under memory constraints in production.

arxiv:2611.02501.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
arxiv:2611.02501.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request, and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.
arxiv:2611.02501.tldr: Presents SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers and optimizes algorithms and systems configurations for speculative decoding deployments.
arxiv:2611.02501.why: Interesting approach to optimizing LLM inference serving efficiency, though specialized for speculative decoding pipelines.

arxiv:2611.02269.title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
arxiv:2611.02269.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.
arxiv:2611.02269.tldr: Proposes Qubrio, a multi-agent LLM framework for quantum compilation and placement optimization.
arxiv:2611.02269.why: Quantum compilation is out of scope for general production LLM applications.

arxiv:2611.02897.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360^{circ} View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments
arxiv:2611.02897.abstract: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360^{circ} scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360^{circ} panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. Project page: https://ntuneillee.github.io/research/photoguider/
arxiv:2611.02897.summary_hint: PhotoGuider selects viewing directions and frames 360° panoramas using shared composition-aware tokens and produces camera-parameter outputs with explanation-conditioned scoring.
arxiv:2611.02897.tldr: Introduces PhotoGuider, a method for composition-aware 360-degree view framing and image cropping using vision foundation models.
arxiv:2611.02897.why: Pure vision and image composition task, irrelevant to text/document enterprise workflows.

arxiv:2611.03219.title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
arxiv:2611.03219.abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.
arxiv:2611.03219.summary_hint: Empirical study shows continual harness self-evolution across software engineering tasks causes severe catastrophic forgetting, with performance on earlier datasets dropping sharply after later evolution.
arxiv:2611.03219.tldr: Investigates continual harness self-evolution in coding agents across multiple tasks, revealing that evolving on subsequent datasets leads to catastrophic forgetting.
arxiv:2611.03219.why: Highlights practical reliability and stability pitfalls when building self-evolving or multi-task agent harnesses.

arxiv:2611.03301.title: An Axiomatic Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
arxiv:2611.03301.abstract: Open multi-agent systems, where only a subset of agents are controllable, are central to real-world domains such as smart grids, yet lack a principled foundation for reinforcement learning algorithm design. We study this setting through n-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT), a recent framework for learning in open multi-agent environments. We propose an axiomatic framework that derives value function learning from the Shapley axioms (Efficiency, Symmetry and Linearity), treating them as structural constraints rather than heuristic design choices. This formulation builds on a novel NAHT decomposition, which characterises the fundamental difference between open and fully controllable multi-agent systems, and establishes a cooperative game-theoretic foundation for learning. We further show that enforcing these axioms on learning individual value functions recovers the Shapley value for Dec-POMDPs, providing a principled bridge between reinforcement learning and classical cooperative game theory. Building on this framework, we introduce Shapley Machines and Banzhaf Machines, two generic algorithmic templates that can be instantiated with standard reinforcement learning methods. When applied to strong base algorithms such as IPPO and POAM, our methods consistently improve learning efficiency and generalisation to unseen agent types and conventions across NAHT benchmark tasks. The code of experiments is published on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/axiomatic-rl-naht.
arxiv:2611.03301.tldr: Proposes an axiomatic framework for reinforcement learning in open multi-agent systems using Shapley and Banzhaf value functions.
arxiv:2611.03301.why: Theoretical multi-agent RL paper with minimal direct utility for applied enterprise LLM orchestration.

arxiv:2611.03008.title: E-GenRM: Generative Reward Modeling for Open-Ended E-Commerce Shopping Agents
arxiv:2611.03008.abstract: We present E-GenRM (E-commerce Generative Reward Model), a generative reward model tailored to e-commerce shopping agents. User expectations are shifting from simple product queries to open-ended shopping tasks. However, existing trajectories and reward designs remain largely bounded by current agent usage patterns and known failures, providing limited guidance for further capability improvement. These limitations call for an integrated reward modeling framework for open-ended shopping agent tasks. On the data side, E-GenRM leverages naturally occurring user behavior across the shopping app to construct diverse, long-horizon conversational trajectories beyond established usage patterns. On the modeling side, E-GenRM first learns from behavior-grounded evaluation chains through supervised fine-tuning. It is then optimized through criterion-guided reinforcement learning, which rewards correct preference judgments and evidence-supported factual claims under each criterion. Personalized hard-negative training further improves its sensitivity to user preferences reflected in shopping behavior, beyond explicit requirements. We additionally develop an active evidence retrieval extension that acquires missing e-commerce information for evaluation. On E-GenRM-Bench, E-GenRM-27B achieves 87.40\% preference accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.97 percentage points. In a 14-day online A/B test on Taobao, a shopping agent post-trained with E-GenRM improves the effective shopping-assistance rate by 1.39 percentage points and user satisfaction by 2.33 percentage points.
arxiv:2611.03008.tldr: Introduces E-GenRM, a generative reward model tailored for e-commerce shopping agents using behavior-grounded evaluation chains and criterion-guided reinforcement learning.
arxiv:2611.03008.why: Too narrow to e-commerce shopping workflows to provide direct architectural patterns for general enterprise applications.

arxiv:2611.02909.title: Cloudra: Geometric Reasoning and Scientific Validation for Autonomous Reaction Mechanism Exploration
arxiv:2611.02909.abstract: Autonomous reaction-mechanism exploration requires proposing reaction steps, preparing three-dimensional structures, and determining which reactant and product a computed saddle point connects. Large language model (LLM) agents can misjudge spatial relationships and confuse a computed structure with the species or step they intended to study. We present Cloudra, a multi-agent framework that constrains mechanistic output through a Delivery DAG of chemical objects. Species nodes carry geometries and bonding topology; elementary-step edges carry transition states and reaction connections between species. Cheminformatics algorithms establish molecular identities and atom correspondences. Deterministic routines measure and transform structures to prepare candidate geometries. Frequency and IRC calculations determine the stationary points found and the species they connect. Agents use these objects to test proposed steps, compare pathways, and revise the mechanism. CloudraBench evaluates the framework's end-to-end mechanism-calculation capability across 50 tasks covering elementary reactions, multistep mechanisms, stereochemical competition, and computational method limitations. Across 200 runs under four workflow configurations, the primary Guided workflow achieves a mean composite score of 0.805, compared with 0.584 for the same-model Standard baseline. On Hard-tier tasks, the Guided mean increases from 0.689 under Standard to 0.958. Under Guided, the self-consistency component reaches its maximum score in 24 of the 40 non-Impossible tasks, compared with seven under Standard. Behavioral analyses examine how the agents use bond and dihedral measurements, optimized structures, and IRC endpoints to revise local mechanistic assignments.
arxiv:2611.02909.tldr: Presents Cloudra, a multi-agent framework constrained by a Delivery DAG for autonomous chemical reaction mechanism exploration.
arxiv:2611.02909.why: Purely domain-specific scientific application (chemistry); the specific verification loops do not transfer cleanly to enterprise RAG or search.

arxiv:2611.02758.title: Learning to Adjudicate: Verifier-Guided Multi-Agent Reasoning for E-Commerce Relevance
arxiv:2611.02758.abstract: Relevance modeling is fundamental to e-commerce search, determining how well retrieved products satisfy the needs expressed in a user's query. Accurate judgments require interpreting user intent, comparing product attributes, and applying business-specific matching criteria. Current methods based on large language models (LLMs) leverage contextual understanding and reasoning, focusing on incorporating domain-specific context and enhancing reasoning performance. Despite these advances, difficult query-product pairs remain challenging when evidence from different perspectives supports conflicting conclusions. A single reasoning pass may fail to reconcile these conflicts and ensure that decisive evidence guides the final judgment. To address this challenge, we propose Collaborative Adjudication with Debate and Replay Experience (CADRE), a framework for evidence-based adjudication in e-commerce relevance assessment. CADRE organizes three expert agents sharing a frozen backbone to analyze product attributes, user intent, and business rules in separate contexts, while a trainable Verifier assesses their supporting evidence against the applicable matching criteria to determine relevance. Under expert disagreement, a Verifier-guided debate elicits targeted clarification and revision of disputed interpretations before final adjudication. We optimize the Verifier through multi-turn group relative policy optimization and adapt successful-experience replay so that trajectories yielding correct terminal labels can be reused alongside fresh rollouts in subsequent updates. For efficient online serving, we use CADRE as an offline teacher to distill its relevance judgments into a lightweight student model. Offline evaluations and online A/B tests on an e-commerce search advertising platform demonstrate that CADRE improves relevance classification and key business and relevance satisfaction metrics.
